column1: # The calls that end processes or delete recursively, file by file, and why each is safe (tests/dangerous_calls_test.py).
# Columns: path, kind, lines, reason. Written from one reading of every line; a count that moves turns the test red.

column4: The folder that mkdtemp made in this routine, checked; no shell; the variable is const.
$! is read right after its &, into the list of the downloads that were started; each number is only waited for; the script sends no signal.
Passes the user's Ctrl-C on to check_proof.py, the one child process that check() has just started, through its Popen handle, which sends nothing once the child has been waited for.

Each signals the session of the child that run_to_the_end() itself started with start_new_session, at the check's time limit, while that child has not been collected: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL for what it started.

check_folder() removes the private folder that it has just made for one check. The sweep removes, in the memory folder and in the jobs directory, only names that begin with this jobs directory's own prefix and that are this account's directories.

One line is a docstring that mentions the shell command "kill -INT" in words. The other three signal the client that the same test started a few lines above: SIGINT through its Popen handle; SIGINT to its process group, which the test made with start_new_session=True and which holds only that client and the stand-in script that it starts, before anything has waited for the client; and, after a time-out, SIGKILL to the same group, reached only after poll() has shown that the client is not reaped, so the ID cannot have been reused.
A two-line shell stand-in for the verifier, which the test itself writes below pytest's temporary directory, ends itself with "kill -9 $$"; it can reach no other process.
Two fixtures kill, by their Popen handles, the stand-in services that they started themselves, and only those that have not exited yet; then they wait for them.

For one test os.killpg is replaced by a wrapper that notes each call, and this line hands on, unchanged, each call that end_to_end.py itself makes (see that file's row); the test chooses neither the target nor the signal. | The test sends SIGINT to its own process (os.getpid()), to see that the handler that main() has just installed stops the run; no other process gets a signal.
Two tests' shell lines read $! right after its &, into a file below tmp_path, to see that the session dies; nothing is signalled by that number here.

For one test os.killpg is replaced by a wrapper, and this line hands on, unchanged, each call that end_to_end.py itself makes (see that file's row); the test chooses neither the target nor the signal.
A fixture and one test kill, by their Popen handles, the stand-in servers that they started themselves, and then wait for them.

Each signals the process group of a program that this script itself started as the leader of a new group (Popen with process_group=0) and has not reaped yet; until it is reaped the kernel cannot give its PID, which is the group's ID, to another process, so the signal can reach only that program and its descendants.

frame_as_the_verifier_reads (two lines): read right after its &; only waited for, never signalled. | Read right after its &; only waited for; build.sh sends no signal anywhere. | One foreground compile stands between & and wait $!; it starts no job here; only waited for, never signalled. | serving: read right after its &; only waited for, never signalled.

only numbers of successful posix_spawn, each its group's leader, are listed; erased under the lock behind waitpid | only under "among && started": a spawned leader, kept unreaped by WNOWAIT; the starting value -1 cannot come here | kill_own_group(): -getpid(), in the supervisor alone, which has first seen that getpgrp() == getpid() > 1, and only once it has started cp_verify. Started by judge_says(), the group was made for it by posix_spawn and holds only what it has started; typed by hand, the group is at most that command line's own job
a shell script in a string, run below a process that the test starts: the script signals itself ($$ is always set and is the script's own process ID)

stop(): the test's own Popen, started in a new session, its process ID checked to be above 1 at the start; killed through the Popen object only while poll() is None, so before it has been waited for (SIGCHLD is set to its default). What that process leaves running is only searched for in /proc and never signalled.

std::filesystem::remove_all, no shell. One removes the folder that mkdtemp() made, by its resolved path, whose last part must be the name just made. The other stands in a faulty stand-in that serves as a control, and removes entries of a staging folder only after the path was shown to lie inside that folder.

A row's group is signalled only while its leader is not reaped (the runner waits without reaping and reaps last; a signal to the runner leaves the leaders unreaped for its handler), so the group's number is still the row's own. SIGCHLD is set back to its default at the start.

In the text of a synthetic row that the test writes: the row's shell writes the number of its own background sleep ($!) into the row's folder; the test only reads /proc for that number to see whether it still sleeps, and signals nothing.

Two are Popen.send_signal(SIGTERM) on the test's own child, the runner it started, by its handle; Python skips a child that it has already waited for. The third, in lives_then_go(), is os.killpg with signal 0, which sends nothing: it asks only whether the synthetic row's process group, named by the runner and equal to the group that the row wrote into its own file in $S (greater than 1 and not the test's own), still has a member; the row then ends by itself once the test creates the file that it waits for.
The test's own child (sleep 30, its own Popen), killed by its handle only if run_suite.end_the_groups() did not end it.

The folder that tempfile.mkdtemp made in this test at line 919, under a new random name with mode 700 in /dev/shm, a place that all accounts share. It is removed only after that mkdtemp succeeded (line 922), in this test's own finally (lines 930-931), and shutil.rmtree follows no symbolic link on the way. No other line sets shm_top: line 919 sets it to None when /dev/shm is missing or the kernel cannot confine the tests, and line 921 sets it to None when mkdtemp fails.
The test's own mkdtemp folder; SMALL_MODEL's folder is read and never removed.

Each $! is read right after its &: at line 351 the call of Lean under timeout, at line 481 the sub-shell that start() has just put in the background. Each number is only waited for; none is sent a signal that ends anything (:352 asks with signal 0; see the kill line).

Line 352 sends signal 0, which ends nothing. The traps at lines 140 and 346 pass a TERM on to this script's own background jobs by job (%N, %%), never by number: bash sends nothing to a job whose process it has already collected, so the signal cannot reach a process that has taken a freed number.

A deliberately harmful command that tools/confine_test.py runs through tools/confine.py alone: it reads $! right after starting its own child with setsid, and it ends that process only after /proc shows that the process's parent is still the command's shell and that the process leads its own group.

A deliberately harmful command that tools/confine_test.py runs through tools/confine.py alone: it ends its own setsid child by the number from $!, only after /proc shows that the child's parent is the command's shell and that the child leads its own process group (the command turns job control off first, so the child cannot be put in a job's group); its other kill calls send signal 0, which checks but delivers nothing, to that child's group, to every process that it may signal (-1) and to the process group that it shares with the test that started it (0).

A deliberately harmful command that tools/confine_test.py runs through tools/confine.py alone: kill -0 -1 (every process of the account) and kill -0 0 (the process group that the command shares with the test that started it) send signal 0, which checks but delivers nothing; the test checks that the signal filter in tools/confine.py refuses the first.

A deliberately harmful command that tools/confine_test.py runs through tools/confine.py alone, and only on kernels whose Landlock confines signals: pkill -KILL -f with a name that the test made unique to its own sleeping child; the confinement blocks the signal to the child, and the test checks that the child is still alive before ending it by its handle; the pattern also matches the command's own shell, whose command line holds the name, and kills it.

A deliberately harmful command that tools/confine_test.py runs through tools/confine.py alone: it tries to remove, through "..", a decoy folder that the test made beside the confined folder; the confinement refuses, and the test checks that the decoy is still there.
The test's own sleeping child (its Popen), ended by its handle after the confined pkill that targets its name has failed to kill it.
$! (line 38) is read right after the & of line 37. It is the process ID of the timeout under which held() has just started its one command, and it is only waited for.

At INT, TERM or HUP the trap at lines 41 to 43 first ignores any further INT, TERM or HUP, so that from then on a second signal does not start the trap again while it runs. It then sends TERM to the script's own running background jobs. It names them by job (%N, the numbers taken from bash's own list, jobs -r), not by a stored process ID: bash sends nothing to a job whose process it has already collected (reaped), so the signal cannot reach a process that has taken a freed ID. The job is the timeout under which Lake or Lean runs; timeout (GNU coreutils, which the script needs) first puts itself and its command into a process group of their own, and passes the TERM on to that group, except in the first few milliseconds after timeout starts: a TERM that arrives then can end timeout without reaching the group, and the command that timeout has just started runs on in that group until it finishes (tools/lean-verify/README.md, "A stray process").

Each $! is read right after its &: at line 61 the timeout under which held() starts a command, at line 276 the timeout under which Lean runs. Each process ID is only waited for; none is sent a signal by number.

At INT, TERM or HUP the trap at lines 67 to 69 first ignores any further INT, TERM or HUP, so that from then on a second signal does not start the trap again while it runs. It then sends TERM to the script's own running background jobs. It names them by job (%N, the numbers taken from bash's own list, jobs -r), not by a stored process ID: bash sends nothing to a job whose process it has already collected, so the signal cannot reach a process that has taken a freed ID. The jobs are the timeouts under which Lake, the parser, the linker or Lean runs. timeout (GNU coreutils, which the script needs) first puts itself and its command into a process group of their own, and passes the TERM on to that group, except in the first few milliseconds after timeout starts: a TERM that arrives then can end timeout without reaching the group, and the command that timeout has just started runs on in that group until it finishes (tools/lean-verify/README.md, "A stray process").

In two stand-ins that the test writes into its own work directory (lines 100 and 128): each writes its own number and that of its background sleep into a file, and the test only reads /proc for them to see whether they have ended. The test itself sends no signal. In twenty calls the timeout command that it starts sends one to the script under test (in seven of them to the process group that timeout made for the script), and would send a KILL five seconds later if the script hung. In seventeen of these calls a stand-in is running when the signal comes, and the script's trap sends TERM on to it through the timeout under which the script started it. In one, the signal comes while the script shows Lean's lines, after Lean's job has ended: the trap stops the script with no verdict. In two, it comes during the script's last checks, after the script has begun to ignore signals, and the script ignores it. Six more calls (lines 861 to 872) run the test itself under timeout 20, which would send TERM to that run's own process group only if it had not ended in 20 seconds.
Not calls: lines 888 and 889 search the two scripts' text, to check that the word kill stands on one line of each script and that this line signals jobs (%N); they send nothing.
A work folder whose name is empty or that already exists is refused. work/tree is made by copytree, which fails on a folder that is there.
A work folder whose name is empty or that already exists is refused, and lay() makes each numbered folder new, so the removal at a pass takes only what lay() made.
work/<name>, made by copytree three lines above; work made new; an empty word counts as existing (it names the current folder).

work/<the call's long label>, in the test's own work folder, which this run makes by a plain mkdir with mode 700, or which is an empty folder of this account's that group and others cannot write; anything else is refused.
Own Popen in Play.one() (the shell execs the program), killed by handle before wait4 reaps it.

Its own Popen in its own session; the test waits for the script without reaping it (os.waitid with WNOWAIT) and signals its group before process.wait() reaps it, so the group's number cannot yet belong to another process.

Its own Popen in its own session, signalled by group after a timeout, before it is reaped. | The handler for SIGTERM and SIGINT signals each running program through a descriptor from os.pidfd_open, opened before anybody waits for the program: it stands for that one process, also once the process has been waited for and its number is free again.
The folder that mktemp -d made (the script stops if mktemp fails); $work is never set again.

Each removes a folder below the test's own pytest tmp_path (Setup's root, set to mode 0700 at :245; fixture setup at :377-378): line 5455 <tmp_path>/spool, the spool folder that the middleware made there when the test started it (:5453; the path at :250), to show that the server then reports a fault; line 6069 <tmp_path>/a/public.aside or <tmp_path>/a/parameters.aside, the test's own folder that swap() renamed aside just before (:6065, swap at :5890), a real folder, not a link; line 6088 <tmp_path>/a/public/leaf, which tree() made at the start of the same test (:6087, tree at :5860-5869, through published() at :5843; the folder itself at :356), a test that swaps nothing. shutil.rmtree follows no symbolic link inside the folder and refuses one given as the folder itself; every folder on the way to these paths was made below tmp_path by the test or, for spool, by the middleware it runs.

SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP, as a terminal sends them, to the process group of the script under test, which the same routine started a few lines above with start_new_session=True and has not yet waited for, so the group's number is still its own; the script is the group's only member.
A cleanup kills, by its Popen handle, the script under test that the same routine started, and only if poll() on the line before has found it still running; then it waits for it.
Handed on to addCleanup on the line after setUp's tempfile.mkdtemp() has made the folder: the test case's own temporary folder and nothing else.
